speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the president of Imperial Oil directly snubbed the twofold request by the Government of Canada that no diversion of Venezuelan oil destined for Canada should take place, and that Imperial Oil establish direct contact with the Venezuelan government rather than operating through its parent, Exxon corporation, in the United States.

That this House asserts that the diversion of Venezuelan oil by the Exxon corporation is not acceptable to the Parliament of Canada and that the government establish immediately Petro-Canada as the sole agency for importing offshore oil into our country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that almost $10 million are raked off every year by the Soviet government from estates of Canadians with relatives in the U.S.S.R., most of it from the disposition of capital from Canadian properties and mortgages, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Parker):
That this government negotiate with the government of the U.S.S.R. full compensation for any properties formerly owned by Canadians and annexed by the allied Soviet government during and after World War II, and also that any past and future estates left by Soviet citizens be transferred to their surviving relatives in Canada, with appropriate legislation preventing Soviet expropriation by means of forgery, duress and excessive overcharging of 45 per cent of Canadian estates left to surviving relatives on their territory.

PARTIES TO CONTRACT FOR PURCHASE OF VENEZUELAN OIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. I should like to remind him of the assurance he gave to the hon. member for Assiniboia earlier this month in which he said, among other things, that Venezuela has been our major supplier, supplying some 40 per cent of our imports. He said he had received personal assurances from Venezuela that those supplies would continue to Canada. Yesterday, the minister also referred to these assurances.
I should like to ask him whether, when he made that statement in the House earlier this month, he knew that the company contracting for these supplies from Venezuela was Exxon, rather than a Canadian company such as Imperial Oil.

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: PARTIES TO CONTRACT FOR PURCHASE OF VENEZUELAN OIL
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, when I was down in Venezuela I raised this matter with the head of Petroleos de Venezuela, the national oil company of Venezuela, and we discussed the contracting relationships which govern the sale of Venezuelan crude to Canada. They pointed out to me that the contractual relationship was with Exxon International, but that they would prefer to deal directly with a Canadian company.
When I got back to Canada I reported to Mr. Armstrong my discussions with Petroleos de Venezuela and the fact that 1 had received assurances of 200,000 barrels a day. Knowing that Imperial Oil of Canada sources virtually 100 per cent Venezuela, I made it clear to him that I wanted him to establish a direct contracting relationship with Petroleos de Venezuela. I put that request to him, for reasons of public policy, in a letter that was sent to him in January.

subtopic: PARTIES TO CONTRACT FOR PURCHASE OF VENEZUELAN OIL
speechtext: I do not know what answer the minister received, but I can guess. Perhaps I had better ask him whether he received a response from Mr. Armstrong and, if he did not receive a response, what he did about it.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. The matter becomes more confusing as the minister ploughs along. Perhaps he could explain to the House what possible benefits will accrue to either the producing provinces which have surplus producibility, or to the Atlantic provinces which obviously need crude oil supplies, by the government's threat to block any further oil swaps by Imperial Oil Limited?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: POSSIBILITY OF SUPPLYING EASTERN CANADA WITH WESTERN CANADIAN OIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think we are in the fortunate position, as I have indicated in the House before, of having surplus producibility in western Canada. The government of Alberta has indicated it is prepared to approve additional liftings of a temporary nature to make up for shortages which are being felt by eastern Canadian refineries. That will be done through the displacement mechanism on a temporary basis. I would expect that these additional liftings in western Canada will be of benefit to and will look after eastern Canadians.
If the hon. member is asking about the threat in respect of Imperial Oil and the concern that might cause to customers in eastern Canada, my answer to him is that if Imperial Oil is not prepared to establish a direct relationship, then it will have to accept the consequences. This is its responsibility to its particular customers, with which it should be concerned. If, as it has said, it has this flexibility to deal worldwide, it should be able to look after them. If it cannot, we are prepared to authorize additional liftings from western Canada to its competitors, and I am sure its competitors will be very pleased to look after that market.

In view of the fact that the minister does not have to wait for that letter from Mr. Armstrong, since he got his answer from the press conference yesterday in which Mr. Armstrong flatly turned down the two requests-one that the corporation deal directly with Venezuela, and the other that they fully restore our quotas-in addition to which Mr. Armstrong said at his press conference that they are going to continue to deal with Exxon and not directly with the government of Venezuela, considering that Imperial Oil took that position yesterday and that Shell, Gulf or Texaco might take it next month or the month after that, will the government not recognize that this is the normal economic performance of the multionationals and, therefore, immediately establish the Canadian corporation, namely, PetroCan, as the exclusive importer of oil into this country?

I cannot as yet announce what the outcome of these discussions will be, but clearly Petro-Canada is in the field right now seeking a contracting relationship with Petroleos de Venezuela in the same way it is negotiating with Pemex, the national oil company of Mexico.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources?
In view of the fact that when this country was in a similar oil crisis in 1973, the present government which was in office at that time brought down the Petroleum Administration Act, committed itself to storing oil in eastern Canada and to set up the machinery whereby it could appoint an allocations committee to control imports and take that out of the hands of the multinational corporations, why has the minister not been using the powers he already has, rather than talking about some nebulous bill which he is going to bring in?
I want to ask him specifically why he has not set up an allocation committee, of which Petro-Canada would be a member, to take control of imports of oil and for dealing with Venezuela. The minister knows perfectly well that Imperial Oil cannot deal with Venezuela if Exxon tells it that it must not do so. When is the minister going to stop being simply a fall-guy for the oil industry and start acting in the interests of the people of Canada?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member referred to the Petroleum Administration Act. That is the act that gives the government of Canada the power to set prices. The hon. member also remembers, as I do, that the official opposition opposed passage of the Petroleum Administration Act. They did not want the Government of Canada to have that power. If they had been successful, Canada today would be paying world prices, not a price significantly below world prices to the advantage of consumers and industry throughout this country.
The hon. member also refers to the allocation powers we had under the emergency supply allocations act. He may also remember that in order to get passage of that important act we had to agree to a sunset clause which was the proposal of the opposition. It goes to show that a sunset clause is not always a very useful provision in an act, because that particular act which gave the power of allocation self-destructed over two years ago.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question of oil storage is an important one. It involves more than Canada; it involves the mutual defence interests of Canada and the United States. The United States has shown an interest, through their strategic petroleum reserves program, in three sites in Canada, two in the Strait of Canso area and one in Newfoundland at Wabana. I believe that three submissions have gone forward on these very significant oil storage proposals.
I can assure the hon. member that as far as storage of oil in Canada is concerned, our storage facilities and our oil in storage right now meets our undertakings to the International Energy Agency.
As to the question of the contractual relationship between Petroleos de Venezuela and Petro-Canada, negotiations started at that time between the two companies. There were discussions with respect to supply and there have been more recent ones. A close working relationship has been established between the two corporations. As I indicated yesterday in an answer, they concern very important areas in the development of heavy oils in western Canada and the heavy oils of Venezuela. Without Petro-Canada it would be impossible, as far as I can see, for Canada to interface with the Venezuelan national oil company. Again the point has to be made that the Tories, who would dismantle and destroy Petro-Canada, have nothing to put in its place.

CUTBACKS IN CANADIAN OIL SUPPLIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), to move the adjournment of the House under the provisions of Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing an important and specific matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the substantial cutbacks in oil supply to Canadians as a result of the crisis in Iran and the action taken by multinational oil companies, particularly the refusal by the president of Imperial Oil late yesterday afternoon to comply with the two requests specifically made by the Government of Canada, namely, that Canada's full quota of oil from that company should be restored, and that this company should deal directly with Venezuela instead of with the parent Exxon Corporation. Such action maintains the shortages of needed oil and contravenes the sovereignty of Canada as expressed through the will of the Government of Canada.
Having moved that motion, I would only add what has been said about the government's intention to introduce the bill, which, in my judgment pertains not at all to the questions that I have raised about the disregard of the multinational corporations of the express wishes of the Government of Canada.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CUTBACKS IN CANADIAN OIL SUPPLIES
speechtext:
Order, please. Both members, as I have indicated, gave me notice this morning of their intention to make this application pursuant to Standing Order 26, and I have to say to them that with my understanding of the purpose of Standing Order 26, as I have said on previous occasions, it always gives the Chair great difficulty to try to resolve these matters and in particular to define whether or not the particular problem which is addressed is of a sufficiently critical or emergent nature to warrant its consideration under this particular Standing Order.
In respect of this particular subject, I would at least be driven to the point of saying that since this matter involves something which is of national scope, it would certainly qualify under those circumstances; and indeed since all parties, under intensive questioning in the last day or two, particularly today, have indicated the very serious nature of the problem, both in the questions today and in the answers given by the minister as to the extent of the problem and the extent of the risk or threat that is involved if the failure to co-operate with the Canadian government's demands goes on, it would seem, on the face of it, to fit the use of the Standing Order.
In the end I have to come to a conclusion, as I have in the past, on two points. The first is that when this House debates Standing Order 26 motions it always debates something of immediate relevance, and I think it is important for the House to do that. Presumably that is the reason for the rule to be on the books, and I do not think we should interpret it so strictly that we can never take advantage of it, otherwise we should take it off the books.
The second point is that in a situation of this sort, when I am left in doubt, I do not see any reasons why I should not resolve that doubt in favour of those who are applying, and I say this freely, particularly so when more than one member makes the application at the same time and when they come from different political parties. This is again an indication of the seriousness with which this matter should be considered.
In these circumstances I am also impressed by answers of the minister which indicate that the government, too, wants it known that it takes this matter very seriously. That was the tenor of the answers given by the minister today. Therefore, it might be helpful to have it known that the House also does take the matter seriously, and therefore it would seem to me to be a useful application of Standing Order 26. That might give some indication of my intention on coming into the House today.
However, the Chair does face a problem in trying to decide whether the situation is an emergency or crisis, because that seems to be somewhat in dispute. I am in great difficulty because of the rapidly developing events. I think likely I would have taken advantage of the provisions of the Standing Order which would have allowed me to set aside some time on the next sitting day, which would have been Monday. I might also have tried to appeal to the House in that some of the strictures of the rule leave me in difficulty. I am not entitled to ask for a debate on whether I should invoke Standing Order 26, nor am I entitled to defer my decision, I have to give today. That is the
February 16, 1979

language of the Standing Order and I think it is appropriate language if the situation is critical. So I think the House understands what I was going to do on coming to the House today.
However, subparagraph (5) of Standing Order 26 provides, as I think hon. members know, that in making my decision under the Standing Order I must have regard to whether or not there would be an opportunity to debate the problem in some other way. If nothing else, the announcement by the minister that he intends to give the House notice of a bill having to do with this subject raises the possibility. I do not know and I have no way of knowing, but the House leader has given an indication, as has the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), that notice of the bill will be given and that it relates to the subject.
Therefore, I am doing the only thing I can do under the circumstances, and that is to set the applications aside today. But I want to say that I do so-and I think the House should co-operate with me in this although I have no procedural way to ensure it-reserving the right of the two hon. members who have involved themselves in this important question to replace the motions, if they wish, at another sitting of the House, after the House has been able to acquaint itself, first, with the terms of the bill, the subject matter it addresses, the scope it provides for debate, and second, with when that debate will take place. These are the two questions we will want answered.
If the bill gives an opportunity to debate the subject in a fulsome way, I will set the applications aside, and therefore I think I should just leave it to the two members. I set them aside today because I have to-I cannot reserve them or defer them. I do that under those circumstances, and I leave it to the House to deal with once it has been better acquainted with the content of the bill and with the timing that that debate may have.

First I should like to point out what everybody already knows. The statistics I have already prove that we have a great growth rate today in the fishing industry. For the 11 months of 1978 to the end of November, the total fish catch was up 18 per cent in volume and 45 per cent in value, a tremendous increase. The landed value was up from $237 million in 1977 to $344 million in 1978. So there has been an increase in volume and a tremendous increase in value.
However, we have to be cautious. The fishing industry has always been a cyclical one. It has always had its ups and its downs; it has always had its three or four good years and then has its three or four poor years. While things are looking good now, we have got to keep that in mind as we approach the future of the fisheries.
There is no doubt that in the rural areas of Newfoundland today there is comparative prosperity, and certainly compared to ten years ago a tremendous prosperity. The rural areas of Newfoundland are dependent completely on the fishery, just as the rural areas of the rest of Canada are dependent upon agriculture. That brings me to my first point. At the recent constitutional conference, the provinces of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland put forward a position on the fisheries at the meetings leading up to it. At the meetings earlier in the year, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) agreed that there would be 14 subjects to be discussed by federal ministers preparing for the constitutional conference of last week. He agreed that one of those 14 areas should be fisheries.
Under the British North America Act today, the fisheries is completely under the constitutional jurisdiction of the Government of Canada, inland and coastal fisheries. That is quite clear; everything that happens in the water is under the control of the federal government. The Prime Minister agreed that this should be one of the 14 areas which could be discussed to see if changes were required and whether agreement could be met.
The striking thing at the federal-provincial conference was that the only one of these 14 subjects that the Government of Canada did not put a position forward on, and the only one where they did not have a position paper, was the fisheries. The government had no position paper on the fisheries, and they made no suggestion as to what changes there should be constitutionally with respect to the fisheries, because the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc), in that petulant display of the power he wields apparently over the government, threatened other government ministers that he would resign if the Government of Canada made the slightest change in its complete control over the fishery.
The second noticeable thing was that of all the 14 topics to be discussed at the constitutional conference, only one was the subject of a propaganda campaign by government ministers going across Canada speaking against it, and that was the fisheries. The minister of fisheries of Canada went about Canada during the period when these ministers were meeting in private sessions. The federal-provincial ministers were meeting with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde). They had three or four or five meetings in between constitutional conferences. The only federal minister who campaigned against any change, or was permitted to campaign against any change, was the minister of fisheries of Canada who spoke in Halifax and everywhere he could decrying any attempt to change complete and absolute federal control over the fishery.
The provinces of Newfoundland and Nova Scotia put forward a proposal that there be concurrent jurisdiction with federal paramountcy for some items of the fishery and provincial paramountcy for others. They suggested the federal government would have paramountcy over international negotiations, surveillance, international enforcement, basic research, conservation, global quotas of fish to be caught, quality standards for export, licensing of foreign vessels; and that the provinces would have paramountcy over determining quotas- inter-Canadian quotas after the federal government determined global quotas, the division of the quotas among provinces-harvesting plans, allocation of aquaculture and fish farming areas, and the licensing of local boats and fishing vessels, with the residual power in the fisheries to be with the provinces.
The minister of fisheries of Canada turned thumbs down on even discussing these proposals for concurrent jurisdiction in the fisheries. He would not discuss them. In his arrogance and his petulance, he threatened to resign if the Minister of Justice or the Government of Canada even agreed to discuss the points put forward by Nova Scotia and Newfoundland and agreed to by all of the other eight provinces. This was a position put on

February 16, 1979

the final day by the ten provinces of Canada. But no, the Fisheries dictator of Canada, the minister of fisheries of Canada, the chief cod of Canada, said "No, we are not going to discuss it."
Now here is an industry. The fishing industry is just as important to Newfoundland as the agricultural industry is to Saskatchewan. There is concurrent jurisdiction in agriculture. The Minister of Fisheries and the Environment is not prepared to concede that there be any mention or discussion of concurrent jurisdiction over fisheries with the provinces.
That attitude has to change. That attitude will change and certainly our party is prepared to discuss these issues with the provinces, keeping in mind that the federal government has to be paramount in at least the areas that were suggested by Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, if not other areas, but that the provinces, like Newfoundland and Nova Scotia, where fisheries is of such fantastic importance to their whole gross provincial products and the livelihood of the people-the whole roary area of Newfoundland with a third of the people living in my district completely dependent on the fishery-these provinces in which these people live should have some say as to what is to happen in the industry.
Here is one clipping to show the position the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment took before the constitutional conference started. He spoke in Halifax as reported on January 27, and said the Atlantic fishermen would be the eventual losers if Ottawa allows the coastal provinces to share in jurisdiction over the fishery. I say "bushwa", Mr. Speaker. That is not proven at all and he has done a disservice to Canada.
One of the arguments the minister uses is that there would be such confusion that the provinces would be competing with one another with disastrous results. Imagine the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment suggesting that there would be any disastrous results about the fishery if the provinces were permitted to have some control, when the federal government has controlled fisheries since 1867 and the fisheries just about died. From the early 1960s until 1975 the fishery nearly expired while the superior minister and his government had full control over it. Canada has had control ever since 1867, yet he turns around to suggest that if the provinces are given some concurrent jurisdiction there is such avarice and such anarchy in the provincial capitals, and there is such incompetence, the fishery would be ruined unless the mighty federal government and this minister have complete control. We are not to have any decisive say in our own lifestyle as to whether our province's economy flourishes or does not, if the present Minister of Fisheries and the Environment is not removed. But he will be removed.
Just look at this: this superior minister who talks so much about federal control being so important sent a release out on February 14 in which he said that fishery improvement loans were up 65 per cent. He said that the federal government under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act had guaranteed 900 loans totalling $16,338,000 during the period April 1,
Government Organization
1978 to September 1, 1978. Last year it was only $9,900,000 but this year it is $16,338,000. This is where the federal government guarantees loans granted by the chartered banks. These loans are not even made by the federal government, yet the minister boasts about these guaranteed loans, made by the banks and not by the federal government, which are up to $16 million this year across the whole of Canada.
Let us look at what is the record of the Newfoundland government in assisting the fisheries and the fishermen. The fisheries loan board of Newfoundland makes loans directly, not through the banks, to the fishermen for boat building, gear purchasing purposes and the like at very, very low rates of interest-I think it is 3 per cent, with very, very low down payments; you only have to put 5 per cent down to get loans from that board to build yourself a longliner, if you are a fit man to build a longliner and sail and operate it. This fisheries loan board of Newfoundland in Newfoundland alone made $23 million in loans to fishermen this year-that is, during the past financial year-as compared to this government guaranteeing across Canada $16 million. The Government of Canada, this mighty government that the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment thinks is so all important to the fisheries, is not doing anything in the line of financial assistance to fishermen. It is not even in the same category as the government of Newfoundland which loaned $23 million in 1,335 loans to bona fide fishermen. Those loans were made in the 1978-79 fiscal year by the Newfoundland fisheries loan board.
That will show the House that the Newfoundland government is taking its responsibilities for developing the fisheries seriously, even though it has no constitutional jurisdiction, and even though it is restricted to doing certain allied and subsidiary things and has no authority over quotas, licensing or what happens in the sea at all.
This government is going to have to decide whether the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment is bigger than the government. The Prime Minister says that one of the 14 topics they will consider for change is fisheries. He is sabotaged by his Minister of Fisheries and the Environment who campaigns across Canada against it, and finally says: Pierre, if you go one iota in this direction I am going to resign, and the great Prime Minister of Canada has to surrender to his little fisheries minister from New Brunswick! That is some spectacle. The Prime Minister of Canada claims he is very, very strong for free enterprise, that the market system is the best system, and yet he has reversed himself in recent years. This is the gentleman whose promises are completely contradicted by his own minister of fisheries, whose policies are not to rely on the private sector at all but to criticize and embarrass the private sector at every stance.
On September 25 of last year they had to write the Prime Minister to point out what the Prime Minister had said and to point out the attitude of the minister of fisheries, his opposition to them, his criticism of them, his refusal to deal with them and his refusal to enter licences for fish freezer vessels, freezer trawlers and the rest of it. The Prime Minister has only given a formal reply to their letter.

One thing this parliament and the Elouse of Commons fisheries and forestry committee will have to deal with-the chairman is here today-is the arbitrary nature of the exercise of power by the minister of fisheries. The minister of fisheries is a man who can make or break you if you are in the fishing business. He can give you gifts of hundreds of thousands of dollars. That is the power that this gentleman has today because he controls licensing, and there are no standards set as to when he is going to give you a licence and when he is not. He can approve of your going into an arrangement with the Bulgarians, if he wishes, with the Russians, the East Germans, the Poles or the Japanese, or he does not have to agree. He can allow this fish company to enter into an arrangement, or he does not have to allow it.
This year I was given, in answer to questions I asked at the committee in November, a list of the co-operative fisheries arrangements, as they call them, for 1978, where the minister of fisheries allowed Canadian unions or Canadian companies to go into arrangements with foreign partners in taking our fish resources in Canada. There is a long list of them. I want to point out that this is entirely arbitrary. If the minister does not like you he does not have to let you enter into that arrangement; he just takes you off his list. Or if he likes you, or if you are a political ally, or if you are allied to the Liberal party, he can allow you to go into a deal.
Just look at squid. The minister did extraordinary things on the quota for offshore squid-not the squid that comes into shore. He gave a gift to various fishing companies in Canada. He said to them: "Look, there are so many thousand tons of offshore squid, we cannot catch it here in Canada. We have not got the vessels for it, the facilities, because it has to be frozen immediately after it is caught. Gentlemen, I am going to give you a licence and you can enter into deals with the Japanese or whoever is equipped to catch squid, and you can sell your right to this licence I am giving you. In effect, you can sell it to the Japanese or whoever wants to buy the squid and you can make yourself $100,000 or $50,000, whatever the amount might be, depending on how much squid I allot to you".
This is the power that we are allowing this individual minister of fisheries. He allowed H.B. Nickerson & Sons Ltd. to take a quota of 4,000 metric tons and they made arrangements with the U.S.S.R. and Japan for these people to catch the squid. The U.S.S.R. and Japan paid them a fee, so much per ton. They did not have to lift a finger. Nickerson did not have to catch it. They did not have to lift a finger, except to make a few commercial arrangements.
It was not just Nickerson. Some 2,000 tons went to Karl Karlsen & Co. Ltd.; 1,600 metric tons went to United Maritime Fishermen Cooperative; 400 tons each went to Ocean Harvesters Ltd., Earle Bros Ltd., Quinlan Bros. Ltd., P. Janes & Sons, of Newfoundland, and to A. Northcott Ltd., Arctic Fishery Products, Port aux Basques Seafoods-400 tons each-and Bay Bulls Sea Products, Beothic Fish Processors, Bonavista Cold Storage and Burgeo Seafoods Ltd. In other words, it was a gift. The minister of fisheries came along and

said to those companies: "Gentlemen, here is a 400-ton gift of squid which you are not going to catch, but you can allow the Japanese to catch it and you can get a fee from the Japanese for that purpose. I am giving you a gift of money." And we are allowing this! There is no board set up to oversee it and there are no rules or regulations to deal with it.
Then he said to National Sea Products: "Gentlemen, here are 6,000 metric tons", and they entered into arrangements with the U.S.S.R., East Germany and Japan. Then he said to Fishery Products Limited in Newfoundland: "Gentlemen, here are 4,000 metric tons. You do not have to put a net in the water, you do not have to send a boat out, you can't because you do not have the equipment, but I am giving you 4,000 metric tons to help your balance sheet this year". I have heard that some of these companies made several hundreds of thousands of dollars just from that alone. The fishermen themselves were allowed the deals through their union. I believe that in some of these deals they were required to process 25 per cent of the squid onshore, and the rest was taken into these freezer vessels and they went off and it was never dealt with in Canada at all.
What about our 7,000 plant workers? Are they to be forgotten in all these deals that the minister of fisheries is in? He is the biggest dealer in Canada. He is big enough to be the biggest in Las Vegas. He is the biggest deal maker the fisheries has ever seen in Canada, and it is all done arbitrarily. There is no principle laid down. It depends on whether you can scratch the minister's back nicely enough. This is a shocking situation and I intend to propose to the fisheries committee that we get right into this.
Now, 3,500 metric tons went to B.C.M. Investment Limited. Who are they? Is this one of Canada's great national companies? All I am able to find out is that there are three individuals who own the company, all Canadians. It is a one-shot deal. They do not own a processing plant. One of the three principals is associated with a small fishing company. Why should B.C.M. Investment Limited be given a gift of 3,500 metric tons of squid, which they sold to Hoko Fishing Company Limited in Japan? This demands explanation.
Another company is Atlantic Sea Products Limited which received 2,500 metric tons. They sold that 2,500 metric tons to Kyokuyo Company Limited in Japan. Who is Atlantic Sea Products Limited? I am told that they have a small fish processing plant down in Hubbards. I do not know what other connection they have with the fishery.
So apart from the large established fishing companies and the smaller ones which were given gifts, there is B.C.M. Investment. They got 3,500 metric tons of squid, 2,000 metric tons of silver hake, which they sold to Hoko Fishing Company Limited, and they got 300 metric tons of Argentine which they sold to Hoko Fishing Company Limited.
What is going on in the administration of fisheries in this country? That is what I want to know, and anyone else who hears this will want to know it too. This minister should not be allowed to give gifts worth tens of thousands and hundreds of
F ebruary 16, 1979

thousands of dollars like this to companies in Canada, or unions or individuals, arbitrarily with no standards set down by this House, no legislation set down by this House or no appeal. You cannot appeal if he refuses you a licence. There is no appeal procedure. There is no appeal court. There is this complete arbitrary use of discretionary power and authority by the minister of fisheries, who is tyrannizing the fishing industry with the immense power that he has. So, Mr. Speaker, I am hoping that the fisheries committee will agree to pursue this.
There are more and more peculiar things going on all the time. The minister of fisheries says that you cannot expand your fishing fleet. "No, I am not going to give you a licence to replace your trawlers; I am not going to allow you to expand your fleet; but I will allow you to enter into all kinds of deals with foreign concerns." When we object to that, he says, "But our Canadian companies can't catch argentine, they can't catch silver hake, they can't catch squid, they are not equipped to do it". Well, how can they get equipped to do it if the minister will not allow them to go into the business of building freezer trawlers? You have to have freezer trawlers to catch these species of fish. He has the industry caught in a vicious circle. He says: "Gentlemen, you can't have a licence for freezer trawler, no, no, no, no." When we object to his giving out all these deals to foreign groups-the East Germans, the Poles, the Russians and all the rest of them-he says: "Well, 1 have to do this because we can't take our quota of silver hake, argentine and the like." We say that he has to start moving now.
The minister is a propagandist. When he spoke here on January 24 he exaggerated what it is we are asking for, what sensible people in the industry are asking for. He said as reported at page 2534 of Hansard'.
Sometimes these protests are accompanied by calls to cash in on this wonderful new bonanza by vastly expanding the fishing fleet.
There is not a soul in Canada asking to vastly expand the fishing fleet, the slaveen; he has just made that up. What we are asking for is the right to replace the fleet that is here now and perhaps expand it a bit; and the right to get some freezer trawlers to catch argentine, squid, mackerel and silver hake, which we cannot do now because we do not have freezer trawlers. The minister went on to say:
In both cases these protests are from people who have not taken the trouble to study the situation or have chosen to ignore the facts for whatever reason.
Nonsense! These protests are by the industry itself and by others who have done a little study in this industry. On the same page he says:
The idea of a massive fleet expansion for traditional species... is a pipe dream.
Sure, it is a pipe dream because nobody ever suggests it except the minister who wants to have something to knock down.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what has he been doing lately? What has this ingenious minister been up to lately, this veritable Santa Claus. He should come in here with a red suit and a white beard. At the moment he has cod on his mind, the
Government Organization
northern cod-2J3K-off northern Newfoundland and Labrador. I was delighted to have the chance yesterday to give recognition to our great new movement in Newfoundland, CodPeace. This movement is the equivalent to cod as Greenpeace is for the rest of the world. It is a movement that wants to protect the cod from the savage seal. This group was initiated by Mr. Miller Ayre of St. John's who deserves a medal. He should get the Canada Medal or whatever it is, like the people who are walking around with these medals crumbling off their chests and bowing them over. It is time that a few of those medals were scattered out where they should go. I propose Miller Ayre right now, immediately, for the whatever it is, the Order of Canada, in recognition of his great movement that will sweep the world-CodPeace. In cod we trust. There is a total allowable catch of northern cod of 170,000 tons. One hundred thousand tons are for the inshore fishery. This is the cod off northern Newfoundland and Labrador. There are 30,000 tons for Canadian trawlers, 25,000 tons for foreign trawlers and 15,000 tons remaining. The minister of fisheries is a dictator, and he has arbitrarily decided that he is going to permit that 15,000 tons remaining in the quota to be caught by foreign vessels so long as they sell the catch to fish plants in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia.
That may be sensible because we do not have special ice-reinforced trawlers that can catch this cod. We are in the humiliating position that we cannot catch our own quota of the offshore, northern cod because we do not have the kind of vessels that will do it, and the minister will not permit the industry to get them. But he is going to permit now the East Germans and the Poles to catch this 15,000 tons as long as they sell the cod, frozen onshore, to our own fish plants for them to process. That is in the circumstance that we cannot catch it ourselves, a circumstance which the minister has put us in. It is the minister who has got us in the position that we cannot catch it ourselves, the Canadian industry. That makes sense, but only because he has forced us into that position.
Fishery Products Limited tried fishing last year and were very successful in catching fish under the ice, up in the ice, but their trawlers are not specially ice-reinforced. They had such heavy damage that the insurance companies forbade them to try that fishery again this year. The East Germans and Poles can catch and land that fish for much less than we can. The minister has not given the trade much time. He did not give them much advance notice. There is a lot of equipment necessary to make this successful so that you can take the frozen products and process them.
My point is this. The minister or the government-and if they don't do it, they will-must announce how they will license in the future in order to permit our present fleets to be replaced over the next five to ten years, the stern trawlers and side trawlers. Our own Fishery Products in Newfoundland has 40 trawlers. They need advance notice because these trawlers

today cost something like $6 million or $7 million. They cannot arrange a whole lot of money in just a couple of months. They must know whether they are going to get one licence next year, two the next or two the next, or however, so they can start replacing the fleet.
The minister has a new policy, which he says he has, and I agree with the concept; he wants vessels owned by individual fishermen or by companies they form rather than by processing companies. I am quoting from his speech which he made in Halifax on January 26. I agree with that concept. It would be better to have our fishing fleet owned separately from the processing companies. They have to know if the minister is serious about this. If he is serious, they are not going to build any more ships. Mr. Speaker, I just have a few minutes to conclude. For the future success and development of our fishery, we need to have growth in the inshore fishery and in the offshore fishery. It is unfortunate that for political reasons the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment and the members of the government have continually stressed the inshore fishery and have seemed to ignore the offshore fishery.
There are 7,000 fish plant workers in eastern Canada who are not going to be able to get a decent year's work; they are going to be on part time work unless we have a successful and

profitable offshore fishery as well as the inshore fishery. So it needs to be balanced. This is the kind of development we need but unfortunately the minister seems to exhibit some prejudice against a strong and healthy Canadian offshore fishery at the present time. If this is the case it is the fish plant workers who will suffer in the long run as well as the fishermen themselves.
It is peculiar the minister should say he is biased in favour of the inshore fishery when his actions in certain areas show otherwise. But now that the fishing industry has become a prosperous one it is time the government started spending some real money on the fishery. We have noticed in my constituency for the last couple of years that the increased emphasis we hear about does not seem to apply when a man is building a long liner. The government is supposed to have a strong bias in favour of the inshore fishery but when a fisherman in Newfoundland wants to build a long liner, a vessel under 75 feet in length-and these have become quite expensive lately, the price running anywhere from $250,000 to $500,000-he can go to the provincial government and get a provincial government subsidy. He can get a loan from the provincial government at an interest rate of 3 per cent. But when fishermen come here for a federal subsidy, they find that the mighty Government of Canada has only $4 million for these purposes to cover the whole of Canada. They discover that the regulations have been changed and that today, before they can get any bounty or assistance for building a long liner, a man has to be replacing a vessel which is at least eight years old.
This is the great federal government which says it is so biased in favour of the inshore fishermen. If that is the case, why aren't they doing anything further to replace these boats? Why aren't they helping new fishermen to enter the industry, men who haven't owned a boat before but who have been fishing for years and are interested in acquiring a boat? It is time for the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc) to put his money where his big mouth is, where his big inflammatory mouth is. It is also time for his colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who bellows like a bullfrog about his great support of the inshore fishery, to see that some real money is put into funds to help fishermen acquire new long liners and new boats for the inshore fishery as well as the offshore. I do not want to mention the Deputy Prime Minister, of course, because he is in the same category; I don't want to hurt his feelings. He is here today and he has called this bill.
We have to remember the plant workers. If the bias of the Minister of Fisheries against the offshore fishery continues, I have three plants in my district, dependent on offshore fishing, the National Sea Plant in St. John's employing some 500 or 600 workers, the Fisheries Products plant in Trepassey, the medium-sized plant in Fermeuse. These plants employ maybe 1,000 workers between them whose jobs on a year-round basis would be endangered if the offshore fleet continues to be neglected by the minister of fisheries.
There are dozens of other plants, inshore plants, which also buy some offshore fish at Bay Bulls, Witless Bay, Arnold's Cove, Admiral's Beach, Branch, St. Bride's, Southern Har-
February 16, 1979

bour, Riverhead. There is a new one going up at St. Mary's, there is Fairhaven-I could name another dozen. We have to remember that when the minister of fisheries "knocks" the industry, when he knocks the offshore fishery, when he shows his bias in favour of the East Germans, the Poles, the Russians, the Japanese and everyone else who fishes offshore except our own national companies which have been taking chances for the last 50 years, before the hon. gentleman was even thought of, he is endangering the employment of all 7,000 or 8,000 fish plant workers in Newfoundland and the Atlantic provinces.
In addition, the minister should spend more money on the inshore fishing villages. There are some 50 or 60 fishermen fishing from Portugal Cove South. That is their whole livelihood. For two years now I have been pointing out to the minister that the wharf and community stage are going into the sea, that the breakwater is crumbling. They are exposed to the sea and if he does not act and start repairs by early April there will be no inshore fishery from Portugal Cove South this year.
Here is an industry whose value is burgeoning. The government is getting greatly increased income from the fishing companies and it is time to use it to increase the funds available for Portugal Cove South, for the work needed at Renews, for the slipway which was promised at St. Shotts, for completion of the work at Come-By-Chance, for the replacement of the wharf at Long Harbour. Peter's River, St. Vincent's, is one of the great inshore fishing commmunities of North America. Peter's River, exposed entirely to the sea, dependent entirely upon human construction to preserve a place to land fish, is a tremendous inshore Fishery; there are inshore fishermen who earned in excess of $50,000 in the six-weeks' trap fishery this year. This is a place which needs a community stage and where the wharf has to be expanded and facilities for landing have to be improved so that the fishermen of St. Vincent's and Peter's River, many of whom are now returning to the fishery, can have the necessary room to Fish and land their catch.
Gaskiers and Pt. La Haye are part of the fishing community of St. Mary's Bay where some of the best inshore fishermen in the province have to land their fish in primitive circumstances. Last year and in 1977 they salted their fish. This year they are landing it fresh. These men deserve help and encouragement. They are building, under the Canada Works program, a magnificent fishing gear storage shed and they are doing the same thing in Peter's River. It shows the value of some of the Canada Works projects. I can assure the minister here today that no projects in Canada are better constructed nor is any of that money better used than at Peter's River, Gaskiers and St. Mary's Bay. If he would like to come with me, or take me down in his jet some time, to Newfoundland-he is only going to have a jet for a couple of months now, until he is bounced out and becomes an ordinary citizen-I would like to show him those two projects. That is where Canada Works funds can really come in handy.

Bay Bulls, Mr. Speaker, is one of the best fishing places in the island and it needs a wharf. It also needs a slipway. These have to be started this year. The minister has promised action for Bay Bulls but has dragged back on his promise for a fishing patrol vessel base. There has been no progress over the last 12 months and we want to know when that work is to start and why it has not got under way as the hon. gentleman promised when the by-election was on. I was elected despite the minister's promises that if the Liberals were elected they would go ahead with this patrol vessel base in Bay Bulls. I was elected and shall be re-elected there very shortly.
I call on the minister now to get this great fishing patrol base in Bay Bulls under way. He should not drag back just because the Liberal candidate does not have a chance, not a hope. He is going to become a powerless third; he might be right off the ballot paper altogether if somebody doesn't take mercy on him and decide to give him the odd vote. The minister should forget politics and just get on with his promises in Bay Bulls to put in the new Crosbie fishery patrol base for the fishing patrol vessels of eastern Canada. If the minister does that I will be very pleased, particularly if he names it after me. That will make me even more pleased.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs, speaking in the chamber on January 25, is reported on page 2561 of Hansard to have said:
I believe that our markets are not sufficiently diversified and are in a more precarious state than is generally realized.
Well, the Deputy Prime Minister is the man in charge of the GATT negotiations. What has the hon. gentleman done to ensure that the worries and fears of the Secretary of State for External Affairs are laid to rest? Apparently nothing. The minister says our markets are not diversified and are in a more precarious state than is generally realized. The government is supposed to be negotiating with the European Common Market to get duty-free or low-duty entry for our fish into the Common Market so we would no longer be almost totally dependent on the United States.
What have the Deputy Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) done to realize this main negotiating point? As far as we can find out, they are being treated with contempt by the European Common Market. Is the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment going to come clean and tell us exactly what is happening in the GATT negotiations? Will it help the Canadian fishermen? Are we going to be able to diversify our markets? It is not enough for the Secretary of State for External Affairs to say he is concerned. He has been in power and in the government since 1968. When is he going to take some action so that we can diversify our markets and not be completely dependent on the United States?
We have a strong fishermen's union in Newfoundland, and that is a good thing and I support it; but I am not going to be completely subservient to the fishermen's union in Newfound-

February 16, 1979
Government Organization
land nor to any other union, and when the fishermen's union of Newfoundland is led by an NDP supporter and when they attempt to get the rest of the members of that union to support the NDP, I have to say I demur.
I have to say that I do not agree, that I think it is a bad mistake for Mr. Cashin and the leaders of the Newfoundland fishermen's union to attempt to get that union to support the NDP. Number one, the membership is not going to support the NDP. They are free-born Newfoundlanders who are not going to be told by anyone whom to support. They are not going to listen to union bosses any more than they listen to company bosses or government bosses. They are free, independent figures, and they are not just going to follow slavishly the goals of the NDP.
So I say yes, we need a strong union, fishermen's union, in Newfoundland. I believe in countervailing power. I think we also need a strong, prosperous fishing industry in the trade of Newfoundland, and I think we need two governments who take a real interest and co-operate in getting the fishing industry going.
I said during the summer that the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment is a puppet of Mr. Richard Cashin, and lo and behold, the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment of Canada wrote a letter to the St. John's Daily News which said, "I am not a puppet". That was the purport of his letter. Imagine the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment having to write a letter to the daily press to say that he is not a puppet. He so appears to be a puppet that when he was called a puppet he had to out-puppet himself and write the St. John's Daily News to say he was not a puppet. He has the appearance of being a puppet, and he does not have the appearance of being fair in weighing the conflicting claims and demands of the trade and the union.
So, Mr. Speaker, I have always been a strong supporter of a good organization for the Newfoundland fishermen. We now have one, but there are certain conflicts of interest in that union which have got to be noted. The interests of the fish plant workers the union represents are not uniform with the interests of the inshore fishermen on all occasions or the offshore fishermen. Many of the deals, for example, that the union entered into last year with the Bulgarians and the Russians did not require any of the fish caught to be landed and processed in Newfoundland, and that is to the detriment of the fish plant workers. And in many other deals of the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment which I recited to the House earlier today that he authorized to be entered into for the catching of squid and the like, the squid did not have to processed in Newfoundland or in Nova Scotia or in Canada, so that Canadian workers lost that kind of work.
This is all pretty shortsighted, and there are many questions to be answered as to what happened last year and whether it was desirable for the arrangements to be entered into that were entered into in the interests of everybody in the industry. The Minister of Fisheries and the Environment says that he is operating in the interests of the inshore fishermen. Well, why, if that is the case, did he take the shrimp resource that belongs

to Newfoundland and Labrador, the great new shrimp resources found off Labrador, and give three licences to his own province of New Brunswick, two catching licences for that shrimp to the province of Quebec, two to Nova Scotia and only two to Newfoundland, this huge shrimp resource off Labrador that rightly belongs to the fishermen of northern Newfoundland and Labrador? And he has retained three of these shrimp licences for fishermen in Labrador who at the present time have no catching capacity. Why did he ignore the interests of the fishermen of Labrador and of northern Newfoundland in distributing these shrimp licences which he now controls in an arbitrary fashion? It takes a huge investment to equip yourself with shrimp-catching vessels for those areas because the shrimp are in deep water.
The result of his action was that Fishery Products Limited could not expand their shrimp processing operation at St. Anthony because two licences were not sufficient for landing shrimp at St. Anthony, and the fishermen of Labrador are now dealing with the minister and trying to take advantage of this resource for themselves. According to my information, at the beginning of February they were getting nowhere with the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment.
The Labrador resources advisory council has made proposals for licences to go to the six communities from Rigolet north to be used in the interests of the people of Labrador. There is a proposal for a co-op to use the licences. There is a proposal for equipment to be put in the plant at Cartwright that might employ 140 or 150 people, but up to February 1- and I have not had a chance to check today because this debate came on quickly and unknown to me-they have had no response from the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment. If the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment is so concerned about the inshore fishermen, why did he take the shrimp resources and divide them up by giving three licences to his own province, two to Quebec, two to Nova Scotia and only two to Newfoundland and three to Labrador?
I might quote from the Union Forum of July, 1978. They call it the single most disappointing decision made in his tenure as Minister of Fisheries and the Environment. They say that this was a political decision and that he is taking away from the people of Labrador and northern Newfoundland the possibility to improve greatly their economic base. I quote from the editorial:
If we are going to start getting into allocating access to lucrative resources on a political basis, then the next thing you know fishermen in Labrador and northern Newfoundland will begin to demand access to the lucrative scallop fishery on Georges Bank.
The union puts its finger right on the problem with this minister. It is politics, and too many of his decisions are based on raw politics. I see that my time is up, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
that Bill C-28, an act to amend the Northwest Territories Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief and in this way I hope to set an example which everyone else will feel compelled to follow.
Bill C-28 is a very short bill which contains only two clauses. It is a bill to which, I can say from the government side, we are prepared to put through all three stages today to expedite it. I have made that offer through private channels and I make it today publicly and await to see if it engenders a response from all opposition parties.
As I said, the bill contains two clauses. The First clause would provide the commissioner in council of the Northwest Territories with the power to alter the size of the council by territorial ordinance from 15 to as many as 25 members. This is a power that the Yukon territorial council has had since 1974. My impression is that this amendment would be supported by all members of the existing council. In fact, this particular provision has been the object of a fairly vigorous lobby in Ottawa by members of the council. They have made their concern known to me, and, I think, to hon. members opposite, that in their view this amendment is in the interests of the Northwest Territories and they ask the House of Commons to move on it. That is why I am prepared to move on all three stages of the bill today, if that meets with the support of the House.
The second clause of the bill would validate an ordinance passed by the commissioner in council at its October session in

February 16, 1979
Northwest Territories Act
anticipation that parliament would enact the bill before us today. The council amendment ordinance empowers the commissioner to describe 22 electoral districts upon passage of this bill, an increase of seven over the presently constituted council of 15 members.
The rationale for the bill is straightforward. Apart from the fact that it has the support of the council and many people in the Northwest Territories, I was able to meet with the new mayor of Inuvik in my office and she told me they strongly support it. I understand Chief Johnny Charlie from Fort McPherson made his views known on radio today and said that he supports it.
I know there are some who have misgivings about it, and I suspect the hon. member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth) may want to develop that; but I think on balance it would be fair to say that the council as presently constituted with 15 members is too small to be properly representative of the cultural and geographic differences of the Northwest Territories. I think it is also fair to say that, given the period of time when we are moving in a very substantive way toward a responsible government in the Northwest Territories, there is a great deal of political communication that must be undertaken, and that can probably be undertaken more effectively by a council of 22 members than one of 15, given the land mass with which the members have to deal, the dispersed nature of the population and the cultural differences.
I think I should also point out to the House that 1 have discussed the bill before us with the special representative of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the hon. Mr. Drury. He studied it and he indicated he thinks it constitutes a forward step and he strongly supports it. Obviously it is a move to reinforce the direction in which I think we are all going toward greater autonomy and responsible government, but it does not-this is a point I should like to stress because it is this point that the opposition, namely, those who wish to be cautious on this bill, are stressing-inhibit constitutional options that would be before us and before the Northwest Territories in the future. I think it is important to recognize that.
The final point I would make is the point about urgency. The statutory life of the council will expire on March 31 of this year and an election must be held soon thereafter. It will be conducted by the chief electoral officer of Canada who, of course, would appreciate as much lead time as possible to prepare for this event. I hope, given the general support that exists for the bill, the argument of urgency, and the fact that the bill in no way precludes constitutional options which we will be exploring, that hon. members will see fit to put this bill through all three stages today.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in this debate. The debate on this bill is long overdue. The bill puts into law what members of the territorial council in the Northwest Territories have been asking for for a long period of time.
We on this side of the House have requested this amendment for some time, but it was not until late last fall that the minister saw fit to bring in the legislation. At that time we indicated to him that we were prepared to give the bill speedy passage, three stages in one day. We are still prepared to do that. We would be very happy to see the bill have three readings today. Unfortunately I understand hon. members of the New Democratic Party are not prepared to give such an undertaking.
As the minister has said, the matter is urgent. Why is it urgent? The answer is very simple. The territorial council have requested this change. Because of the vastness of the territory they represent, the council feels it is not realistic that there should be only 15 members on the council. They feel they cannot represent adequately the people who are scattered throughout the territories.
Approximately a week ago I was in the territories and had occasion to talk with members of the territorial council. I spoke with one councillor who told me that, in order for him to visit one isolated community, he had to charter an aircraft. For him to charter an aircraft, spend the day in the community and fly back cost approximately S500. He also indicated that he had a number of such communities in his constituency. One can see it is almost impossible for 15 members to represent properly the people in the area. This is the feeling of the members of the territorial council.
In anticipation of an increase in its numbers, the council passed an ordinance on October 27, 1978 which provided for the setting up of 22 different ridings or constituencies and for the provision of 22 members to represent those constituencies. Clause 2 of the present bill provides for retroactive approval of that ordinance. As the hon. minister pointed out, the life of the council in the Northwest Territories expires on March 31, 1979. This is why members of the territorial council came to Ottawa prior to Christmas. The minister said that they were lobbying, but I do not feel, when members of a provincial government or a territorial government come to Ottawa to talk with either the minister or opposition members, that they are lobbying. I feel they are doing their job; they are attempting to represent their provinces or tneir territory.

It is unfortunate that the New Democratic Party has not seen fit to undertake to give three readings to this legislation today. In talking to members of the legislative council last week, they indicated that it is very possible, if this legislation does not receive quick consideration, they will have to proceed with their election under the old provisions of the act. In other words, there would be an election of only 15 members rather than 22, and another four years will go by before there could be proper representation on the council.
I am disappointed in one respect regarding this bill. For some time the territorial council has asked the minister to change the legislation. Rather than the council being called a

February 16, 1979

council, it would be called an assembly; and rather than being called members of the territorial council, the members would be called members of the legislative assembly. Unfortunately the minister has not seen fit to include that provision in the bill.
This bill is an important one because it gives better representation to all areas of the territories. There are those people in the north who say that the territorial council does not represent all the people of the north. But if one examines the make-up of the present council consisting of 15 individuals, one will find that nine of those 15 councillors are native people.
Last week when the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) and myself were in the territories, we met with the territorial council for approximately two hours. At that time one of the territorial councillors posed the following question: "Some of the people say to me that I do not represent the native people. What do you people think?" We asked him about his constituency and his constituents. It was practically made up of native people. We responded to him by saying that under a democracy, once a person is elected by secret ballot, he represents all the people in his constituency whether or not they voted for him.
If one examines the attitude of the government over the years, it would appear that the government and the minister do not believe that the duly elected territorial council, the representatives of the people, in fact represents the people of the territories. One may ask why I say this. It is very simple. The government and the minister have refused to allow the territorial council or representatives of the territorial council to participate actively in the land claims negotiations.
This goes for the Yukon as well. I understand representatives from the Yukon were in Ottawa a week or two ago. They were members of the newly elected government in the Yukon. They asked the minister to give them the right of representation in the negotiations which will be and are taking place with the natives in the Yukon concerning land claims. When the COPE agreement was negotiated, at least the agreement in principle, it is interesting to note that it provided for the setting aside of roughly 10,000 square miles of the Yukon Territory on the north slope of the Yukon and that there was no prior consultation with the territorial council in the Yukon respecting that land. Representatives of the territorial council in the Yukon read the COPE agreement and found that the Government of Canada had set aside some 10,000 square miles on its own.
I suppose this land is owned by the people of Canada, but basically it is owned by the people of the Yukon. It was set aside without the properly elected people or the legislators in the Yukon having an opportunity to have a say in it.
I suppose that at some time in the future the government will say in respect of the COPE agreement that the territorial government had some input because the commissioner of the Northwest Territories signed this agreement. The commission-
Northwest Territories Act
er acts under the direct authority of the minister. He does not act under the authority of the government of the Northwest Territories, and he signed the agreement under the instructions of the minister and not under the authorization of the territorial government.
I want to make it perfectly clear that any reference I have made to the COPE agreement has nothing to do with the contents, which will come up sooner or later in parliament for consideration. I will reserve my comments on the agreement until that time. I use that as an example of the manner in which the Government of Canada, not only this minister but ministers of Indian affairs and northern development in the past, deal with or treat that area.

speechtext:
We on this side of the House are always interested in the truth, and if there is information that has come to light recently to which we are not privy I would certainly be very happy to listen to what the minister has to say when that is possible.
The government over the years has consistently treated the Yukon and Northwest Territories as colonies. The minister in his remarks a few moments ago made some reference to the granting of responsible government. I suggest that this government has no intention of ever granting provincial status, for example, to either of the territories, because the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) of this country within the last year made that statement. He said the territories would not have provincial status during his lifetime.
It is interesting to note what the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson) said when he spoke during the referendum debate on January 31.1 quote from page 2774 of Hansard as follows:
Let us look at the Yukon. The Conservative party now is committed to giving provincehood to the Yukon. What does that mean? It means provincehood to the Northwest Territories shortly after, and eventually it means turning over the

February 16, 1979
Northwest Territories Act
natural resources of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories to extremely small populations. That policy was enunciated by the Leader of the Opposition and the Conservative party. If that is the position of the Conservative party, the Liberal position is somewhat different. The government considers the natural resources of the north are the common heritage of all Canadians.
Those are the remarks of the hon. member for Laprairie. This legislation today enlarges the legislature. I feel that, regardless of the attitude of this government to the territorial council, this change means greater representation to the people in the Northwest Territories, and, whether the government likes it or not, it means a step toward self-government and provincial status for the N.W.T. Self-government cannot evolve without a settlement of native claims, and the territorial governments, whether in the Yukon or the Northwest Territories, must be a part of these negotiations.
I have a copy of a speech made by the distinguished member of the territorial council, the Hon. Arnold McCallum, in the legislature of the Northwest Territories on February 1. He was replying to the commissioner's opening address. I should like to read a short part of what he said as I think it is important. He said:
I rise to talk about the most important contemporary issue facing this Legislature. And, in talking of it, I rise to make what I think is the most important speech I have ever made in this House.
I do this because I sense that we are approaching an intersection, a point at which all of us in the Northwest Territories-native and non-native-may push ahead to a better social order, or doom ourselves to the back-burner, and throw away our main chance to embrace in the N.W.T. what the rest of Canada takes for granted-self government.
I believe that the route we choose depends on whether we as members of this Legislature behave as politicians seeking personal or partisan gain-or whether instead we become statesmen.
I believe that if a free Northwest Territories is to emerge, that if a free Northwest Territories is to evolve, we must then become statesmen, wise in the science of government and unselfish and conciliatory in our conduct and in our work.
It is for this reason that I want to speak to you today, and speak to all citizens of the Northwest Territories about a species of wildlife.
It comes to light later that the species of wildlife to which he refers is government bureaucrats. He goes on to state:
The federal intent in land claims is to divide and conquer, and to divide and conquer us all.
In now agree with the Indian Brotherhood of the N.W.T. I now agree with the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada. I don't agree that the federal government is the culprit. As I've said, I believe the federal bureaucracy is. But I do agree with these groups as to what is happening: Divide the peoples of the Northwest Territories and, by so doing, conquer and control the peoples of the Northwest Territories.
This speech received little if any coverage in the southern press. It is an important speech and I believe it expresses the opinions of many northerners. It is a speech of some 30 pages. I do not know if the minister has read it, but I recommend it to him. Certainly it should be made compulsory reading for all senior civil servants in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. It recites a scenario in the north of divide and conquer; a divisive policy at a time when we should be doing everything possible to unite our country. I do not blame the minister. He is only one of four whom we have had in the past six and a half years that I have been here. He has a heavy and responsible portfolio. The short period of time

which the various ministers have spent in the portfolio makes it impossible for them to grasp completely what is happening. They must depend on senior civil servants for advice.
The future of our country depends on the attitude and policies of the government, not only toward the native people, but toward all the people of the north, and in particular the elected representatives of those people. Fortunately there will be a federal election soon. I say that that election will bring about a change in government, and under a Conservative government there will be the development in the north envisaged by the former Prime Minister, the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert, which will be based on the spirit of co-operation between all northerners regardless of background.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to make some remarks on Bill C-28, the bill which is before the House at this time, and I am pleased to follow the two previous speakers who remarked on this bill, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Faulkner) and the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil).
I am concerned about the number given to this bill. It seems to me that that is the number which the government uses to bring in bad legislation. I am sure that hon. members will recall that the last time we had to contend with a bill C-28 it was the bill which, in effect, restricted collective bargaining for civil servants.
I was surprised to hear the hon. member for Moose Jaw say that he would like to see this bill pass third reading today. I consider the bill to be nothing but a piece of window dressing on the part of the government. It does absolutely nothing for the autonomy of the north. I believe that the hon. member for Moose Jaw said that we would have to wait another four years before they-and I assume when he said they that he was referring to the people in the Northwest Territories-will get proper representation. I am quite sure that the many good members sitting on the N.W.T. Council would take offence at that remark, and I hope that that is not what the hon. member meant by the statement.
I would be more than happy to support a bill which would bring autonomy to the north. I have represented that beautiful part of the country in this House for a little over six years, and during that time I have been waiting and hoping that the government would bring in legislation giving us the autonomy we are seeking. This bill, however, does not do that, and that is why I do not think it should be treated so lightly. The bill in its
February 16, 1979

present state should not even be on the floor. If it had the substance which would bring some autonomy and a responsible government to the Northwest Territories, then I would be the first one on my feet to muster support for it, but not the way it is. All it does, as it stands, is put a few more seats on the territorial council.
If the government wishes to change the name from Northwest Territories Council to the Legislative Assembly of the Northwest Territories, that is no problem. The only cost involved is to rewrite a few lines to change the act. Not too long ago I introduced a private members' bill in an attempt to do that very thing, but the government did not seem to get too excited, nor did they voice their support.
I made some statements about this proposed legislation when I became aware of it a few months back. I put out a press release stating my views. Basically the theme of that press release, which I put out in June, 1978, was that "bigger is not necessarily better." I am sure that there are a large number of people in the Northwest Territories who agree with me, although I know that the minister has been able to quote accurately some people who are in favour of this increase in the size of the Territorial council, and that would be fair enough if they were given more responsibility to handle some of the very important matters and questions which have to be answered.
Many hon. members will remember the recent news reports from the communities of Rae/Edzo in the Northwest Territories. It was a prime example of the drastic housing situation there that was brought to light through an outbreak of tuberculosis, a disease which is commonly associated with the poverty stricken people of the world. I have harped on this situation since I have been a member of this House, but what I have been saying on behalf of my people on matters of this nature have fallen on deaf ears.
Now the Liberal government and the party to my right here are willing to take a little piece of legislation, give it all these fancy-sounding, kind words, and say that it is good for the north, that the people up there are asking for it, and "we will give it an hour and a half or two hours on a Friday afternoon to put it through all three stages, and rubber stamp it." They feel that that will keep the people of the Northwest Territories quiet for a while and make it seem as though they are getting some autonomy.
No matter what the results are of the next election, whether we have a Conservative government or a Liberal government, the situation will remain the same.
